tldr: Integrating vision-based lane perception and a reinforcement learning running policy onto the commercially available humanoid Unitree G1 achieved fully autonomous track running in real races (100 m, 400 m, and 1500 m). The work reveals that compensating for camera shake, interpolating odometry across flight phases, and actively managing motor heating through pacing are crucial to finishing.
overview:
In recent years, reinforcement learning has enabled humanoids to run robustly. However, there have been few demonstrations of a complete autonomous running system that perceives lane lines and completes an actual race on a track without human intervention. Accurately tracking lanes using vision alone, navigating curves at an unfamiliar venue, and pacing within hardware limits requires system-level integration far beyond basic locomotion control.

Rather than developing specialized athletic hardware from scratch, the authors equipped a commercially available life-sized humanoid, the Unitree G1, with an extra compute board and camera, entering it into the 100 m, 400 m, and 1500 m events at the World Humanoid Robot Games (WHRG) 2026. While building upon lane detection techniques from autonomous driving, they developed algorithms to tackle two violated assumptions unique to humanoid running: severe head-camera oscillation and the flight phase where feet leave the ground.

Furthermore, the biggest hurdle during real-world running was actuator (motor) heating. Without countermeasures, the robot suffered thermal shutdowns and fell after just 50 m. The team introduced a three-tier thermal management strategy: penalizing torque during training, adding heat-dissipation plates, and applying temperature-based speed limiting. As a result, except for a single fall caused by a lane-detection error in the 400 m semifinal, the robot successfully finished all its races in the 100 m, 400 m first round, and 1500 m.
contributions: Demonstrated fully autonomous track racing at an international competition using a commercially available Unitree G1 humanoid by integrating lane perception, path tracking, and RL-based running control.
Achieved stable lane tracking during humanoid running via image stabilization and horizon leveling against severe head-camera shake, alongside leg odometry that bridges flight phases using an IMU.
Proposed a comprehensive thermal management approach combining RL reward penalties on actuator heating, physical heat-dissipation plates, and real-time temperature-based speed limiting (pacing).

sections.heading: More than just running: the grueling challenge of autonomous track racing
sections.summary: While humanoid locomotion control has advanced, integrated systems that autonomously detect lane lines at an unseen venue and finish within hardware limits remained unexplored. The authors used an off-the-shelf Unitree G1 to tackle multiple events fully autonomously at WHRG 2026.
sections.details:
For a humanoid to compete in track events, simply maintaining upright locomotion is far from enough. The robot must step onto an unseen track not present in training data, reliably track lane lines around curves using onboard sensors alone, avoid burning out its motors, and finish in a high-stakes, single-attempt race without restarts.

Key underlying technologies have seen remarkable progress, including lane detection in autonomous driving, onboard vision navigation for legged robots, and deep reinforcement learning for bipedal running. However, system-level reports detailing a humanoid navigating an actual competition track fully autonomously while managing both visual perception and thermal constraints have been exceedingly rare. While some humanoids have completed half-marathons, they relied on custom hardware or liquid cooling, leaving their autonomous software stacks undisclosed.

In this work, the authors avoided building a specialized machine, opting instead for a system built around the commercially available Unitree G1. Competing in the 100 m, 400 m, and 1500 m events at WHRG 2026 in Beijing, the robot placed 13th of 74 in the 100 m (24.3 s), 10th of 44 in the 400 m first round (1:55.93), and 7th of 35 in the 1500 m (7:43.89). This paper openly shares their pragmatic, battle-tested system design and deployment results, detailing how they overcame severe running vibrations and thermal bottlenecks.

sections.heading: A sharp-curved speed skating track and strict competition rules
sections.summary: The track events at WHRG 2026 took place on a makeshift track laid out inside an indoor speed skating oval, featuring tighter curves than standard athletic tracks. The rules enforced full autonomy, banning any external intervention after the start signal.
sections.details:
The competition took place on an athletic track laid directly over an indoor speed skating oval in Beijing. Because it repurposed the speed skating layout, its curve radius was significantly tighter than that of a standard 400 m track. For the robot, this meant a shorter forward sightline and severe geometric constraints, requiring sharp direction changes with a tight turning radius.

The authors entered the Small Humanoid category (height under 1.4 m) for the 100 m and 400 m, and the Open category for the 1500 m. The competition rules were strict: all external wireless communication via Wi-Fi or RC controllers was strictly prohibited after the start, requiring all steering commands to be generated autonomously onboard. The only human intervention permitted was sending the initial start command immediately after the starter pistol, and official race times included the latency of that manual operation.

sections.heading: Tailoring an off-the-shelf Unitree G1 for track racing
sections.summary: The 29-DoF Unitree G1 was upgraded with an Intel RealSense D555 head camera and a Jetson AGX Orin (PC3) for vision processing. Perception and control were cleanly decoupled through a simple velocity and yaw-rate interface $(v, \omega)$.
sections.details:
The base platform was the Unitree G1, a commercially available humanoid robot with 29 degrees of freedom. While the robot comes with two internal compute units (PC1 and PC2), the team mounted an external Jetson AGX Orin (PC3) to handle the heavy computational load of lane perception and path tracking.

The stock head camera was replaced with an Intel RealSense D555, chosen for its wide field of view and durability. To prevent USB disconnection under heavy running vibration, they used a wired Ethernet connection. The camera captured RGB and depth frames at $1280 \times 720$ resolution and 15 Hz. PC3 detected lane lines and computed target forward velocity and yaw rate $(v, \omega)$, transmitting them via ROS 2 to the internal Jetson Orin NX (PC2). PC2 executed the RL running policy and thermal limiting module to command joint torques.

By condensing the boundary between perception and locomotion into simple $(v, \omega)$ commands, the team could tune the RL running policy independently via remote control before integrating the autonomous stack. In addition, custom heat-dissipation plates were attached to critical motors. These hardware additions added only 1.5 kg, keeping the robot's weight to 36.5 kg compared to its 35 kg specification.

sections.heading: Running breaks assumptions: adapting lane perception and path tracking
sections.summary: Adapting autonomous driving lane detection to bipedal running broke two core assumptions: smooth camera motion and continuous ground contact. These were overcome via IMU-based image stabilization and horizon leveling, paired with flight-phase leg odometry.
sections.details:
Directly applying autonomous driving techniques to running bipedal robots breaks two core assumptions that hold true for passenger vehicles: that camera motion is smooth, and that wheels maintain continuous ground contact for reliable wheel odometry.

### IV-A Lane Perception
To select a detector, the authors qualitatively evaluated GANet, BezierLaneNet, UFLDv2, and CLRerNet on stadium imagery. CLRerNet proved the most stable due to its use of global visual context. Because athletic track lanes are narrower than roadway lanes, keypoint-based methods often conflated adjacent lane markings on low-resolution feature maps. Using a ResNet-34 backbone, the network was fine-tuned on 3,000 real-world frames collected across 30 outdoor tracks with an action camera, along with 300 synthetic frames rendered from a simulated replica of the venue. Accelerated with TensorRT (FP16), inference took 17.6 ms per frame, enabling stable 15 Hz operation.

However, during running, head-camera roll rotated violently with an RMS of 2.0 to 3.3 degrees, causing lane lines to tilt drastically in every frame. Furthermore, camera pitch pitched the vanishing point far away from the training distribution. To fix this, an IMU-based preprocessing step leveled the image via a pure-rotation homography based on the estimated orientation from a Madgwick filter before feeding it into the detector.

Directly tracking lane lines in image space remains prone to occlusions by other robots or transient false detections. The authors projected detected lane lines onto the ground plane estimated from depth images, accumulating them into a 0.2 m voxel grid in the odometry frame. Fitting a cubic polynomial to aggregated observations up to 18 m ahead of the camera provided highly resilient tracking.

### IV-B Path Tracking
On the odometry side, the G1's default state estimator flipped velocity sign estimates with every step during running, underestimating forward speed at around 1 m/s because stance detection lingered after foot-off. The team implemented custom kinematic leg odometry that detected stance based on foot height and bridged the flight phase using IMU integration. On a 400 m practice track, it logged 377 m (a 0.94 scale factor), providing sufficient accuracy for lane following.
For path tracking, Vector Pursuit (an extension of Pure Pursuit) ran at 100 Hz with a 6.0 m lookahead distance and a 16.5 m minimum turning radius. This allowed the robot to navigate tight curves without decelerating, staying cleanly within the controller's yaw rate limit of $\pm 0.4\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.

### IV-C Venue Adaptation
The competition venue was darker than outdoor environments, featuring non-uniform ceiling lighting and floor reflections. Because on-site retraining carries a high risk of unexpected regression, the team refrained from retraining at the venue. Having already achieved domain adaptation using synthetic images, they simply locked camera exposure and gain manually on-site to verify perception stability.

sections.heading: Reinforcement learning for running: curbing heat and withstanding torque fade
sections.summary: Training used a three-stage RL curriculum combining PPO and Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) in Isaac Lab. Penalizing hip-pitch torque minimized motor heating, while feedforward torques and randomized thermal degradation boosted real-world robustness.
sections.details:
### V-A Policy Training
The running policy maps high-level target velocity and yaw rate $(v, \omega)$ to target joint positions for all 29 joints, plus feedforward (FF) torques on selected joints. Training in Isaac Lab followed a three-stage curriculum: PPO, AMP using human running data, and final PPO fine-tuning. Early experiments without AMP quickly saturated hip-pitch torques; imitating human sprinting mechanics successfully resolved this torque saturation.

Because the hip-pitch motors ran hottest during real-world tests, the reward function included a penalty on squared hip-pitch torque as a proxy for Joule heating alongside velocity tracking. Actuator thermal dynamics are difficult to simulate accurately, so temperature was excluded from observations and rewards. The policy ran at 50 Hz using proprioceptive histories, while PC2 interpolated target positions to 1 kHz to drive the motors. The team trained two policies: a straight-line sprinting policy for the 100 m, and an endurance policy supporting turning commands for mid-distance races.

### V-B Hardware-Aware Policy Design
The hip-pitch and knee joints—the primary drivers of forward propulsion—were assigned relatively low PD gains (10.0 to 15.3 N·m/rad) and received direct feedforward torque outputs from the RL policy (whereas hip roll and yaw used 100 N·m/rad). Driving these joints purely through position tracking would require the PD spring term to generate large propulsion forces inefficiently, whereas feedforward torques enabled more efficient actuation.

Additionally, motor torque constants decrease as actuators heat up (torque fade). To counteract this, a first-order thermal model was introduced into dynamics randomization, degrading the torque constant by up to 28% based on accumulated torque load. Although the policy could not directly observe this degradation, it naturally learned robust locomotion capable of sustaining running even as motor torque faded.

sections.heading: Heat was the primary rival: a three-tier defense and event-specific pacing
sections.summary: Without mitigation, motors shut down from overheating after only 50 m, making thermal margin the primary speed bottleneck. The team deployed a three-tier thermal strategy—training penalties, cooling plates, and runtime limiting—tailoring pace to each race distance.
sections.details:
### VI-A Heat as the Speed Bottleneck
When sprinting humanoids at full power, the primary speed bottleneck was not dynamic stability, but motor heating. In baseline tests without thermal countermeasures, the motor firmware's thermal protection tripped after just 50 m, cutting power and causing the robot to fall. Finishing each race depended entirely on how strategically the available thermal margin was spent.

### VI-B Three-Tier Thermal Management
The team tackled motor heating across three distinct levels:
- **Policy Level (Training)**: The reward function penalized squared joint torques, encouraging relaxed, energy-efficient running mechanics.
- **Runtime Limiter (Deployment)**: Peak MOSFET temperature across all joint motor drivers was monitored in real time. If any driver exceeded 120°C, the speed limit was gradually dialed down to 2.0 m/s over 4 seconds. If temperature reached 127°C—just short of the 130°C firmware hard cutoff—a safe stop command was issued. Path tracking received this updated speed cap and recalculated yaw rate to maintain the target curvature.
- **Hardware Level**: Custom heat-dissipation plates were mounted to the hip-pitch, knee, and ankle actuators, effectively shunting heat away from the motors and into the robot's aluminum frame.

### VI-C Event-Specific Pacing
Because heat accumulates continuously while running, pacing strategies varied with race distance. The 100 m sprint used a high-speed profile that consumed the full thermal margin. The 400 m race used a conservative pace until the home stretch, where the speed cap was raised to 5.0 m/s for a sprint finish. For the 1500 m, a modest, constant speed limit was maintained from start to finish to avoid triggering the thermal limiter.

sections.heading: Battles at WHRG 2026: finishes, strong ranks, and a semifinal pitfall
sections.summary: At WHRG 2026, the robot completed three out of four races: 13th in the 100 m, 10th in the 400 m first round, and 7th in the 1500 m. However, a lane detection failure caused a fall and DNF in the 400 m semifinal.
sections.details:
### VII-A 400 m: Strong First Round and Semifinal Heartbreak
In the 400 m first round, the final sprint kicked in at 90.4 s, bumping the speed cap from 4.0 m/s to 5.0 m/s on the home stretch. The robot finished in 1:55.93, placing 10th of 44 and advancing to the semifinals.
However, just before the semifinal start, visual lane tracking exhibited abnormal jitter. Lacking setup time to recalibrate, the team had to start the race. Roughly 5 seconds in, the robot cut diagonally across the lane to the right, tripped, and retired. Because an onboard recording glitch prevented flight logs from saving, the root cause could not be conclusively proven, but it is suspected that a fall during morning practice bent the camera mount downward, shifting the image vanishing point. Learning from this, the team added an emergency projective transform before the subsequent 100 m sprint, using camera IMU pitch to center the vanishing point.

### VII-B 1500 m: 7th-Place Finish on the Brink of Overheating
The 1500 m was an extreme test of thermal endurance. Starting at 53°C, driver temperatures rose steadily, peaking at 119°C at 460.6 s—just 1°C shy of the 120°C runtime limiter and 11°C below the 130°C emergency cutoff.
Although the target velocity was set to 4.0 m/s, estimated speed from leg odometry averaged 2.98 m/s, yielding an official average speed of 3.23 m/s (official finish time: 7:43.89). Of 35 entries, only 7 finished without falling or overheating; the G1 secured a strong 7th-place finish.

### VII-C 100 m: Full Sprint Hits the Thermal Limiter
In the 100 m sprint, the robot set off at maximum speed (5.6 m/s target). At 22.1 s, driver temperatures crossed 120°C. The runtime limiter activated immediately to lower the speed cap, and temperatures peaked at 123°C, successfully preventing a 127°C shutdown. Finishing in 24.3 s (13th of 74), the robot narrowly missed qualifying for the next round, but proved that the runtime thermal limiter could save the hardware under full sprint conditions.

sections.heading: Four lessons for deploying commercial humanoids in the real world
sections.summary: Completing three international competition races with an off-the-shelf Unitree G1 yielded four vital lessons for real-world deployment: perceptual robustness, flight odometry, venue adaptation, and thermal management.
sections.details:
Taking humanoids out of controlled lab environments and onto a competition track revealed four crucial lessons for real-world autonomous deployment:

- **1. Vision resilient to aggressive body motion and occlusions**: Running causes head-camera roll oscillations of 2.0 to 3.3 degrees RMS. IMU-based horizon leveling and projecting lane lines into an odometry-frame ground voxel grid enabled continuous lane tracking across all recorded race frames without dropouts.
- **2. State estimation across flight phases**: Bipedal running introduces flight phases where both feet leave the ground, breaking standard wheeled or walking odometry that assumes continuous contact. Detecting stance via foot height and bridging flight phases with IMU integration is essential.
- **3. Venue adaptation without on-site retraining**: Retraining deep neural networks on-site under tight deadlines poses major regression risks. Covering domain shifts beforehand using synthetic venue replicas and locking camera exposure and gain on-site proved far safer and highly effective.
- **4. Hardware-aware policy training and thermal management**: Sustained running without burning actuators requires a layered thermal defense: torque penalties in RL training, physical heat sinks, and real-time temperature-based speed limiting.

These four takeaways offer practical design principles for future humanoid systems operating in challenging, real-world environments.

sections.heading: Appendix: leg odometry, training setups, and dynamics randomization
sections.summary: Implementation details of leg odometry, lane tracking voxel grid parameters, AMP training using human motion capture data, and thermal model hyperparameters for torque degradation are detailed here.
sections.details:
### Leg Kinematic Odometry Implementation and Accuracy
The odometry module registers foot stance whenever foot height stays within 2 cm of its minimum over the preceding 0.8 s. During stance, kinematic velocity (weight 0.8) and IMU predictions (weight 0.2) are fused, while flight phases rely solely on IMU integration. On a 400 m practice track, the estimated distance was 377 m (scale factor 0.94). Analyzing logs from the 1500 m race, cumulative lap distance estimates over three laps were 352.3 m, 345.1 m, and 349.3 m (standard deviation 1.0%), showing high consistency. The estimated mean curve radius was 24.20 m (actual design: 26.49 m), resulting in an aggregate distance scale factor of approximately 0.90 including tracking offset and heading drift.

### Lane Detector Training and Tracking Parameters
CLRerNet was trained with an input resolution of $960 \times 960$. The training set comprised 3,000 real outdoor track frames and 300 photorealistic synthetic images rendered via Gemini (gemini-3.1-flash-image) from a simulator venue model. In ground-plane tracking, 0.2 m voxels decayed by a factor of 0.95 each frame, fitting a cubic polynomial once 8 or more voxels accumulated. Voxels beyond 5 m behind, 18 m ahead, or 8 m laterally from the camera were pruned, and jumps in odometry exceeding 2 m triggered a tracking reset.

### Running Policy Training and Rewards
During the AMP stage, motion data was sourced from seven 50 m sprints (240 Hz) captured from two runners using IMU mocap suits. Trajectory translations were scaled to match the humanoid leg length ratio (0.85 to 0.91), preventing unnatural crouched running gaits. The reward function penalized squared torques across the hip-pitch, knee, hip-yaw, and ankle joints to prevent localized heat buildup. It also imposed penalties on mechanical power ($|\tau \cdot \dot{q}|$) and an L1 norm on feedforward torques.

### Thermal Degradation Dynamics Randomization
To simulate real-world thermal fade, a first-order lag model was introduced into simulation, reducing the torque constant by up to 28% based on the ratio of squared torque load. Model parameters were sampled from uniform distributions per joint. Withholding this degradation state from the policy encouraged the emergence of robust running gaits capable of withstanding degraded actuator torque on the physical robot.

takeaways: In real-world bipedal running, actuator thermal margin—not dynamic stability alone—is the true governing bottleneck for maximum speed and running distance.
Humanoid running causes violent camera shake and intermittent ground contact; porting autonomous driving stacks requires IMU-based image leveling and flight-phase odometry interpolation.

Adapting to an unseen venue via on-site deep network retraining carries high regression risks; combining prior synthetic domain adaptation with locked camera exposure and gain on-site is far more reliable.

In reinforcement learning controller design, penalizing squared torques, adding feedforward torques, and simulating thermal torque fade via domain randomization are critical for real-world deployment.
limitations: Due to the single-attempt, high-stakes nature of the competition and the risk of falls, detailed on-robot ablation experiments isolating individual system components could not be conducted.
Because onboard logging failed during the 400 m semifinal, the hypothesis that a physically bent camera mount distorted the vanishing point and caused the fall remains experimentally unproven.
The motor thermal model implemented in simulation (up to 28% torque constant reduction and time constants) was based on empirical assumptions rather than direct physical thermal bench measurements.
